passages.t: The school of the wilderness: ‘man does not live on bread alone’
passages.happening:
Moses calls the people to keep every command, so that they may live and enter the land (verse 1). Then he tells them to look back.

“Remember that these forty years the LORD your God led you all the way in the wilderness, so that He might humble you and test you in order to know what was in your heart, whether or not you would keep His commandments” (verse 2).

“He humbled you, and in your hunger He gave you manna to eat, which neither you nor your fathers had known, so that you might understand that man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD” (verse 3).

In all that time their clothes did not wear out and their feet did not swell (verse 4). “So know in your heart that just as a man disciplines his son, so the LORD your God disciplines you” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The forty years in the wilderness were a sentence. A generation died there for refusing the land. Moses now shows the same years from another side. They were also a school. God ‘led you all the way’.

Two verbs describe what God was doing. He humbled Israel, and he tested it. The word for ‘humble’ can mean harsh treatment, as in Egypt. Here it means bringing down self-reliance so that trust could grow. The word for ‘test’ means to prove something, to bring out what is really there.

The lesson was taught with food. For an ancient farmer bread was life, and the Hebrew word for bread often stands for all food. In a world where famine was always near, Moses says that bread is not the deepest thing a person lives on.

Manna was the flaky food that appeared on the ground each morning. Exodus explains its name from the question the people asked when they first saw it: ‘What is it?’ Neither they nor their fathers had known it. They could not grow it or explain it. They could only receive it. And it could not be stored. What was kept overnight spoiled, except on the day before the Sabbath. By its nature it taught Israel to depend on God one day at a time.

So the sentence in verse 3 does not despise bread. God gave them bread. It says that behind the bread is the word of the one who gives it, and that a person lives by that.

The picture of a father and son in verse 5 belongs to the ancient household. Training a son was a father's duty and a sign of love. It was not rejection. Moses asks Israel to read its hardest years as the care of a father and not as the anger of an enemy.

That is a reading Moses gives of Israel's own history, looking back. It is not a key for explaining every hardship in any person's life.
passages.later:
Exodus tells of the first morning of the manna: ‘they asked one another, “What is it?” For they did not know what it was’ (Exodus 16:15).

Jesus, hungry after forty days in the wilderness, was told by the devil to turn stones into bread. Jesus answered, ‘Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God’ (Matthew 4:4). Israel, called God's son, was tested in the wilderness for forty years. Jesus, the Son, was tested there for forty days. He would not use his power to feed himself apart from his Father's word. He trusted where Israel had grumbled.

Jesus later spoke of the manna and of himself: “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger” (John 6:35).

The letter to the Hebrews takes up verse 5: “For the Lord disciplines the one He loves” (Hebrews 12:6).
passages.hard:
Verse 2 says God tested Israel ‘in order to know what was in your heart’. If God knows everything, why did he need to find out?

Readers who confess that God knows all things have understood the words in a few ways that fit together.

Many take them as language shaped to human understanding. God is spoken of as coming to know in the way a person does. The testing brought into the open what was already true, and it did so for Israel's sake and not for God's.

Others note that the Hebrew word for knowing often means to experience or to acknowledge, and not only to gain a fact. On this reading God is said to see Israel's loyalty proved in real life.

A few theologians argue that the text shows God truly learning from human choices. The wider Christian tradition has generally not accepted that view.

The chapter itself stresses the purpose of the test. It was not a trap. It was meant to humble Israel and, in the words of verse 16, ‘so that in the end He might cause you to prosper’. The test showed Israel to itself.
passages.asks: Moses tells Israel to look back at its hardest years and find God's leading in them. Ask whether there is a hard stretch of your own life in which, looking back, you were being taught to trust. And ask what you really live on. If the thing you depend on most were taken away, ask what would be left.

passages.t: A good land, and thanks after eating
passages.happening:
Moses describes what lies ahead. “For the LORD your God is bringing you into a good land, a land of brooks and fountains and springs that flow through the valleys and hills; a land of wheat, barley, vines, fig trees, and pomegranates; a land of olive oil and honey” (verses 7-8).

It is a land where they will eat without scarcity, ‘where you will lack nothing’, with iron in its rocks and copper in its hills (verse 9).

One command goes with it. “When you eat and are satisfied, you are to bless the LORD your God for the good land that He has given you” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
After the desert, the list reads like a song. To people who had drunk from a rock and eaten the same food for forty years, Moses speaks of running water and seven kinds of produce.

The description fits the land. Its water came from springs and seasonal streams, and not from one great river like the Nile. Its staple crops were the ones named here: wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives and honey. The honey probably includes the syrup of dates as well as the honey of bees. Jewish tradition calls these the seven species. Copper was mined in ancient times in the dry valley south of the Dead Sea.

Notice that Moses is not afraid of good things. The land is good, the food is good, and being full is good. Nothing in this chapter says that plenty is wrong. The gift is to be enjoyed.

What he adds is verse 10. When you are full, bless the LORD. Thanks turns a full stomach into a memory of the giver.

Jewish practice built on this verse the grace that is said after meals. It keeps the lesson of the chapter at the family table, at the moment when a person is most likely to forget.
passages.later:
Jesus gave thanks over bread before he fed the crowds: “Taking the five loaves and the two fish and looking up to heaven, He spoke a blessing” (Matthew 14:19).

Paul tells the rich where good things come from. They are to put their hope ‘in God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy’ (1 Timothy 6:17).
passages.asks: Moses commands thanks at the moment of fullness. Ask when you last thanked God after a good meal and not only before it, or after a good year. And ask whether you can enjoy what you have been given without guilt, and still remember that it was given.

passages.t: ‘The power and strength of my hands’
passages.happening:
Now the warning. “Be careful not to forget the LORD your God” (verse 11). The danger will come when they have eaten and are full, when they have built fine houses, when herds, silver and gold have grown. ‘Then your heart will become proud, and you will forget the LORD your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt’ (verse 14).

Moses reminds them again of the desert: the snakes and scorpions, the thirst, the water from the rock, the manna (verses 15-16).

Then he names the thought. ‘You might say in your heart, “The power and strength of my hands have made this wealth for me”’ (verse 17). “But remember that it is the LORD your God who gives you the power to gain wealth, in order to confirm His covenant that He swore to your fathers” (verse 18).

If they forget God and go after other gods, they will perish, like the nations before them (verses 19-20).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is built around two verbs, remember and forget. It also has a shape. The wilderness is remembered at the beginning and again near the end, and the good land stands in the middle. The hearer is led from the desert, into plenty, and back to the desert, so that plenty is seen in its light.

In Deuteronomy, to forget is not to lose a fact. Israel will always be able to recall God's name. To forget God is to live as though he had not acted. It is a failure of loyalty, and the cure is deliberate remembering.

Moses traces how it happens, one step at a time. First there is food, then a fine house, then growing herds, then silver and gold. Then the heart is lifted up. Then God is forgotten. No one decides to do it. It comes with comfort.

Verse 17 is the turning point of the chapter. The proud heart tells itself that its own hands made this. Moses does not answer that work is worthless or that wealth is evil. He answers that even the strength to work is a gift. And he gives the reason God gives it: to keep the promise he swore to the fathers. Israel's wealth is evidence of God's faithfulness, and not of Israel's merit.

The closing warning sets Israel beside the nations. If Israel forgets its God, it will go the way of the peoples it replaced. Being chosen is no shield.

This passage is about the pride of those who have plenty. It says nothing against the poor, and it does not say that wealth proves God's favor or that poverty proves his displeasure.
passages.later:
The prophet Hosea saw the warning come true: “When they had pasture, they became satisfied; when they were satisfied, their hearts became proud, and as a result they forgot Me” (Hosea 13:6).

Paul puts Moses' answer as a question: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

Jesus told of a rich man who talked only to himself about his full barns. God said to him, ‘This very night your life will be required of you. Then who will own what you have accumulated?’ (Luke 12:20).
passages.asks: The thought of verse 17 is said ‘in your heart’, where no one else hears it. Ask what story you tell yourself about how you got what you have. Then think of the strength, the mind, the health and the chances that made your work possible. Ask how many of them you made yourself.
